text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz S1 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones With Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod Update: Changing tips really improved these phones. The tri flange tips really hit the sweet spot in my ear. I can 'tune' the bass now by how far I shove them in my ears.

Still not for critical listening but a very easy to listen to headphone. Cymbals sound better now. Bass is more balanced with good extension/bloom for < $100 IEM's. They are forgiving of poor source material and/or using with portable electronics. They strike a good middle ground between musical and detailed, though it's somewhat a case of not doing either one particularly well but that's getting nit picky.

The phones are bit bulky and heavy and the cord bounces while running. I also find I tend to futz with them a lot while wearing them. Adjusting the fit, playing with the cables, etc. But all and all they fit well and stay put for most activities. The thicker/flat cord bothers me at times. It always feels like it's going to come off my ears but in reality it doesn't. I think with more wearing they will drape nicer over the ear.

But to my ear they still lack 'something'. If I had to do it over I'd probably try the NuForce 700's or Thinksound ts02/MS01.

Upping my rating to 4 stars for being perfectly good, if some what uninspiring phones.

Original review:
Too thumpy and not in a good way. It's all, ok mostly boom with no 'good' thud. (I'm guesing there are even boomier headphones I out there.

I got them an hour a go and I already know they are going back.

And I like bass and I like warm and forgiving over 'accurate' and 'lively'.

I like the $22 Vsonic GR99 better than these. Though to be fair these are 'technically' and are better in the treble than both of them but it's not enough to offset the excessive bass for me and again I like bass. If you want to hear not just the bass drum but also the beater side of the bass drum these are not the phones for you. If you like the sound of all the drums, including the rack toms, these are not for you.

If you want to hear bass instruments that sound like they do in real life, these are not for you.

They are so V-shaped they sound like they have hole in the frequency response. If you know what that means and feel like you hear that kind of things these are not the phones for you, if like me you are being swayed by the number of good reviews.

If you think 'beats' sound good you might like these. If you 'bump' in the car and or like hip hop/rap than you might like these. If you are coming from crap phones you might like these because they probably have better highs and more bass extension (rumble I see people call it and rumble it is, and not in a good bass extension way). If your frame of reference for drum sounds is EDM you may very well like these.

I'll be returning these and sticking with the GR99 until I can find something better. I don't think these are worth the $60 they cost based on owning Vsonic VC02 and Vsonic VSD1's (which I really liked but just couldn't get a good fit).

While the highs have fairly nice extension and no sibilance or tizzinesss don't expect to hear the metal of the cymbals, mostly you get the sound of the tip of the drum stick on the cymbals. But that is pretty common until you get to better phones/speakers. While not expensive the Vsonic VC02 was very good at 'cymbal' sounds.

These are v-shapped to the point of sounding like they have hole in the frequency response. If you know what that means and think you can hear such a thing, these phone are definitely not for you, in case like me you are being swayed by the number of good reviews.

Do they sound 'terrible' no, unless you have heard better. Do not get these if you are looking for good phones with a little more bass than what you have now I like I was trying to do over the Vsonic VC02. I like the VC02 but wanted something with more bass to use while working out. I also like my Vsonic VSD1's but I put them through the wash and never could get a very good fit, so I'm not replacing them.

I was worried about these and the bass sound but wanted to try them since I almost always wear phones with the cord over my ears. and in that aspect they are pretty comfortable and were easy to fit and get a good seal with the stock size tips. They feel a little big to me but I'm coming from Vsonic VC02 which are very small.

All music was 320k MP3 or FLAC using the DAC headphone amp in the Topping VX1 amp using foobar 2000.

If accurate reproduction of bass sounds, including drum sounds is important to you look else where.

I like BASS. The GR99 are bass heavy as are the Skull Titans. The Vsonic VSD1 are not shy of bass compared to other phones, but the bass sounds more natural on those even though they are bass heavy in comparison to accurate/neutral phones.

I'm being generous giving them 3 stars but 2 stars felt too low since so many people like them and mine is just one opinion. One persons and one person's boomy is another person's good bass extension.
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz S1 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones With Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod

text_fidelity_a:
HP 20-inch LED (1600 X 900) LED Backlit Monitor with VGA & DVI-D Port (W2082a, Black) - L8K84AA#ABA This is a decent PC monitor that doesn’t excel in any area but, at the same time, doesn’t fall flat either (except for sound quality). It’s a good choice if you’re looking for an inexpensive, wide-screen monitor that comes in at under $100.

The build quality is what you’d expect at this price point: pretty basic and simple. The casing is all plastic, and rather cheap feeling plastic at that. It comes with a very basic stand that allows a limited amount of tilt adjustment, but no swivel or monitor rotation. There are no mounting holes on the back to facilitate a wall or stand mount. There are also no convenience features, such as a USB hub. It also lacks an HDMI port.

On the plus side, the power cord just plugs into the monitor without the need for a transformer or wall wart. The overall monitor profile is pretty slim, and it is very lightweight.

Setup is very simple. No tools are needed to attach the stand (just push and it clicks into place). It comes with a VGA cable, a 3.5mm audio cable and a power cable. Although it includes a DVI port, it does not come with the cable to use that. It also does not come with a user guide (other than a one-page quick setup sheet) or a driver disk. Both are available as downloads from the HP site. However, neither are really needed.

I hooked it up to my laptop via VGA to use as a secondary monitor. It auto installed under Win 7, so it should be able to do the same for 8 and 10. The recommended resolution is 1600x900 at 60Htz.

Right out of the box the settings were eye-searing bright, as is typical with manufacturer defaults since they want their monitors to stand out when on display in a store. Changing the settings is pretty easy – the menu button brings up the full list of options; you select the one you want; then adjust with the +/- keys. You can experiment at will since there’s also a choice to return to factory defaults should you get lost in the weeds with changes. The adjustment menu is pretty extensive for a monitor at this price point. You can adjust the usual brightness and contrast, and also color temp, image control, and even turn off the blue LED power indicator (yes!). Unfortunately, the control button labels are impossible to read (black on black) but there’s only a few buttons, so it's not tough to figure out.

The image quality is decent once it’s been properly adjusted. It won’t wow you, but it provides good performance on both images and text. I was happier with the text performance than I was with video (it has pretty limited black levels) but, for an everyday, inexpensive monitor, it’s more than acceptable.

The speakers are very, very basic. Tinny to the point of being useless. I’ve gotten better sound out of a $5 set of basic computer speakers.

I’m giving this 4 stars since, even at this price point, HP could have done a better job with the overall look/feel of the monitor, have included some additional convenience features such as a swivel, USB hub, and/or an HDMI port. Features that could have been dropped are the internal speakers, which are useless for anything other than to hear system beeps. Still, even as-is, it’s worth considering if you’re looking for a no-frills, no-fuss, inexpensive monitor.
text_fidelity_b: HP 20-inch LED (1600 X 900) LED Backlit Monitor with VGA & DVI-D Port (W2082a, Black) - L8K84AA#ABA

text_fidelity_a:
Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer Overall, this is a solid charger. The build quality is top-notch, it’s sized so that you don’t have to struggle to put in/take out 26650s, and the 3A charge rate is a treat. However, it has a design issue that, while not a major roadblock, can be quite irritating.

Let’s start with the good news. This is one solidly-built charger. Compared with other chargers in its general price class from Efest and Xtar, this has a lot more heft to it. The sliders are perfect – not too loose; not too tight – and move smoothly without any crunchiness or squeaking. Best of all, it can hold two 26650s without any difficulty getting them in or out of the slots. That’s a great feature since I’ve been using a lot more 26650 mods recently, and getting those fat batteries in or out of some of my Xtar chargers is a major pain.

Other ease of use features include non-slip feet on the base that keep it firmly planted. The included power cord does not have a wall wart on the end – just a regular plug – which is a welcome change. All in all I have absolutely zero complaints about the fit and finish.

Performance is also solid. Each slot is independent, and can be set to charge at up to 3A. However, only one channel can be set at 3A since the total cannot exceed 5A. But even one 3A channel is a great feature if you use large capacity 26650s that can support a 3A input. It cuts the recharge time to the bone. It also has a USB output for charging (2.1A). However, you must leave slot 2 empty if you want the USB charging to take priority. Otherwise, it will charge the cell in slot 2 first, then charge via USB.

The charger has all the customary protection features that you would expect from a good quality charger such as overtime protection, reverse polarity protection, and auto shut off if it runs more than 10 hours. It also has a recovery mode for deeply discharged Li-ion cells. I never use that (if I accidently deeply discharge a cell I no longer use it) but it has the feature should it be of value for your needs. Heat output when running was very low.

The current for each slot can be set to 0.5A, 1A, 2A or 3A. You can also set the cutoff voltage to 1.2v, 3.7v, 4.2v or 4.3v. I use this nearly only with Li-ion cells, so the 4.2v cutoff is what I use for most of my charging. However, it’s nice to have the 3.7v setting for when I want to charge cells for long-term storage.

If you do nothing, the charger will set itself to a 2A current for cells that are greater than 1200mAh, and 0.5A for cells less than 1200mAh. You can override the settings for both current and cutoff independently for each channel.

And that’s where the biggest irritation occurs. The charger has a double row of LED lights that signify current and cutoff levels (plus blink to show operation, and stop blinking when charging is done). Simple and unobtrusive. However, there are no notations on the screen to show what charge rate/cutoff corresponds to each LED. Instead, those numbers are listed on a piece of clear plastic that is stuck on top of the display. It peels off easily and looks like a temporary cover to protect the screen.

In addition to looking poor, the lack of durability of the cover with the numbers listed means it won’t survive for long. Now, there are only four positions for the LEDs so it’s not a huge puzzler to decipher the settings if you use the charger regularly. However, I have several chargers and can go a couple of weeks between using one in particular. It can be hard to remember which LED position means what. And I shouldn’t have to do that – numbers should be imprinted right on the screen and not on a flimsy piece of plastic.

I also don’t care for the fact that the button labels (one for current, one for cutoff) are embossed into the plastic. The black-on-black makes it very hard to see which button is which.

But those issues aside, this is a solid charger that offers up to 3A charging. The build quality and operation are both excellent, and it’s perfectly sized to hold two 26650 cells without a bit of struggle to get them in or out of the slots. The poorly designed screen and button labels drops my score to 4.5 stars, but I’ll round up since everything else is well executed.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer

Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology [[VIDEOID:fab011cbaf4d8ff273fb360a6d075448]] My granddaughter is too young to remember the big bulky Polaroid instant camera, so when I showed her this camera and told her it took instant pictures that she could use as stickers her comment was "AWESOME", and she's dying to get her hands on it. This compact sized 10 megapixel camera offers users the option of printing 2" x 3" photos instantly or adding up to a 32 GB micro SD card in order to store or share images.

The camera is straight forward and simple to use. If you want to take instant photos just load [[ASIN:B00ZSPI3A6 Polaroid 2x3 inch Premium ZINK Photo Paper TWIN PACK (20 Sheets) - Compatible With Polaroid Snap, Z2300, SocialMatic Instant Cameras & Zip Instant Printer]] into the chamber in the back of the camera, remove the magnetic lens cap, and gently press the viewfinder to turn the camera on.

Using the selector wheel at the top left, you can choose to take your photos in color, black & white, or sepia (which is like old time tin type for an antique look). Choose one, and then press the button next to that to select whether you want the photo to have a border or not. You can even press another button on the top to activate a 10 second delay to take selfies, and there's also a "photo booth mode" which takes a series of six quick pictures over the course of 10 seconds that you can set by depressing the shutter for three seconds.

Once you've chosen all of your desired options simply frame your shot in the viewfinder and press the shutter. There's no zoom or available adjustment, the camera automatically focuses and uses flash if needed, and the 2" x 3" print comes out of the side of the camera clear, sharp, and dry to the touch in under a minute. If you have film loaded the camera is going to print photos automatically when you press the shutter, so don't load paper if you prefer to use the micro SD card and not print. The camera has an auto sleep function that will shut it off to save battery power if sufficient times lapses between use, or you can just press the viewfinder back down to shut it off manually.

There are no instructions that comes with the camera, but you can read or print the manual yourself by going to polaroidsnapcamera dot come. You can also find the firmware update there. Be sure to charge the camera fully when you receive it, then insert a Micro SD card and update the firmware before using it. (Available here: http://polaroid.com/products/polaroid-snap-camera) Besides printing paper, you'll definitely want to have a MicroSD card for the camera and a case: [[ASIN:B017A1D6TI Polaroid Neoprene Pouch for The Polaroid Snap Instant Camera (Black)]].

There are several things about this product that could be improved on:
1. No sample printing paper included
2. No picture preview
3. No strap to attach the lens cover to which would help prevent losing it
4. Viewfinder pops open too easily
5. No instruction manual or link mention of the firmware update (or link to it) included with product

Otherwise, the camera is well made and fun to use. I can see where kids would have a lot of fun with this camera, but the photo paper isn't cheap so I may let my granddaughter use some and then just mostly use the Micro SD card. This could also be useful for producing instant photos at special events such as birthday parties, weddings, proms, and for other occasions, and the peel off backing on the photo paper makes it nice for scrap booking.

This instant camera was provided at no cost for my evaluation and review.
text_fidelity_b: Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology

text_fidelity_a:
Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black My SX280 HS is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 lens errors. This is the closest replacement, AFAIK. The 40x zoom is probably not that useful, since the 280's 20x was right at the limit of stable framing, but no biggie. I just like the SX HS series with the DIGIC 6 processor. I looked at the 730, but didn't need Bluetooth & didn't like the look of the oversimplified controls. And $50 buys a couple of extra batteries.

One thing you do get for several years of technology development is a better battery/sensor. Thus far the 720 shows no sign of gobbling electricity the way the 280 does. The extra $100 also buys a better written manual. I discovered a couple of minor features both cameras have, but which you'd be hard pressed to figure out from the 280's manual.--9/2/2017
Update: The 280's video/battery life problems are fixed in the 720. Image stabilization is very good. I got acceptable results at >20x zoom with a light-weight monopod (a Slik). Close focus also appears much better.--9/4/2017
I'm still on my first battery charge!--9/17/2017
Update: I fixed the 280's lens errors with a can of air and a heavy hand blowing out the gaps in the lens. Risky, but it worked. The 720 is still my go to camera. I upped the rating to 5.
July 2019 Update--I got a killer deal on a Panasonic Lumix ZS70. Great camera ... but ... it feels a lot bigger than this one in my hand. It has more features, does more things, but the 720 is lighter, handier, and in some cases takes better still pictures. If you don't need an EVF, tilt-screen and better video, this (or its SX740HS successor) might just be the better choice. The 740 has a tilt-screen.
June 2020
One word of advice. The sensor is 20 Mpx. The lens is capable of delivering 5-8 Mpx. This is typical of these small cameras. Don't be afraid to use lower resolutions or higher compressions. You won't lose much. Still a favorite camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black

text_fidelity_a:
Sennheiser Momentum Headphone - Brown I've had several pairs of Sennheisers before the momentums namely a pair of HD580's from back in 1999 & much more recently a pair of HD650's. Let me start off by saying I'm not an "audiofile" I'm not a headphones snob. I don't name drop as to act like I know everything about all "cans" as they're referred to as. But I do know music & I know MY TYPE of music, which is pretty much everything except Country/Western. I listen 100% through my iphone or iPods.

I come from an LP, then 8 track (yuck), then cassette, then CD background so when I finally went all compressed format I didn't realize what I'd be "missing" I just thought, "Wow what a convenience"!! Anyway, I ended up ditching all my CD's (about 1400 total, originals!) & ripping them into iTunes, total of about 7500 songs. I long ago sold my HD580 back in 2005 & just listened from earbuds. I got tired of these real quick. So I saved up & did my research & just knew I had to have the Senn HD650's but I knew I had to have a good amp so I bought both (used) & I was thoroughly disappointed. I didn't hear this "wide open" expanded 3D imaged sound that everyone bragged about. After "damning" these headphones for being overpriced I realized, after my anger, I was being angry at the wrong item, it wasn't the can's it was the compressed format that removed all the subtle nuances of the original recordings!

So back to the drawing board to look for a decently priced (new) set of headphones. I bought a pair of in ear headphones from Sennhesier of course & these sounded good, better than than the Apple buds. Then I ran into the Momentums! I did my youtube & google research & the Momentums appear to be the one's I've been looking for. It has the controller but are "can" style headphones not earbuds! The cord is just long enough so i can stick my iphone in my pocket but no so long that it'll get caught on a doorknob or something else. The only drawback is it was hard to find the black with red from any type of discount. I got the brown ones reluctantly but I couldn't argue the price I got them for and for what it's worth the brown looks pretty clean & euro with the brushed aluminum.

I knew as soon as I started listening to some of the typical songs I play that I found my pair. They're paired perfectly for the portable MP3, phone or tablet's. You don't need an amp of any kind, they have great sound quality even for a sealed back design an because they're sealed you won't bother anyone sitting next to you at moderate levels. I was kind of put off of how small the ear surroundings were because my ears are not huge but they do stick out a bit, once I found a good position my ears fit fine.

All I can say is that I"m finally happy with a pair of headphones. I think the challenge is to match your style of music with headphones. Don't listen to name droppers & snobs who only talk about Gredo, AKG's HiFiMan & even Sennheisers. People knock Beats by Dre but hey if your music is like 99% current day hip hop & Dance then the Beats are probably the best suited for you. They're not for people who listen to live rock or classical. I had to find that out the hard way those higher priced headphones that require DAC's & AMPS aren't necessarily suited to my music. I believe the momentums are a great "in betweener" set of headphones. For that person who's aged a bit where they're not looking for LOUD & BOOM any more, they know & want detailed sound but they're still at a stage where they're listening to their music in a compressed 256k or less format, mp3 or wave format & not CD's anymore, but want that CD sound brought back.
text_fidelity_b: Sennheiser Momentum Headphone - Brown

LensPen NLP-1C Lens Cleaner (Black with Gold Rings) This lens pen is just what I need in a compact, easy-to-carry product. I am a photographer who has to carry a lot of gear outside. Having something compact and light is essential.

One side is a brush to get rid of fine and large particles of material from the lens. The other side is to remove oils (e.g. fingerprints) and is made of a fine material that has a carbon dust cleaning solution embedded in it.

The first three to five uses can be a bit frustrating as this carbon dust is quite heavy and will actually leave a slight residue on the lens. In this case I just used the brush first, the carbon cleaner second, and then finished up with the brush again to remove any extra carbon. I had no artifacts in my photos at all. After the initial break-in period this lens pen performs flawlessly.

The pen is close to 4 inches long (without the brush extended) and about 3/4 inches wide. Its actually very compact and light. It has a tab on the cap to be able to secure it while its in a pocket, just like a regular pen. The brush is about an inch long and is used by extending it out of the end of the pen. It adds about an inch of length when extended. The carbon cleaner is covered by a cap which is screwed off in order to expose the cleaning surface. I wish there was a spot to put this cap while using the carbon cleaning side. Its the only long term con to this pen.

Pros:
*Light
*Compact
*Cleans lenses well
*Easy to carry in pocket
*Cheap

Cons:
*Carbon dust residue for first 3-5 uses.(-1/4 star)
*Cap has no place to be put on the pen while using it. (-1/4 star)

Overall 4.5/5 (>=.5 rounds up, <.5 rounds down) => 5 star rating

If you have any further questions regarding the product in my review please leave a comment below and I will get back to you as soon as possible.
text_fidelity_b: LensPen NLP-1C Lens Cleaner (Black with Gold Rings)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Washable Wired Keyboard K310 I often eat at my desk, which is not the greatest thing. Croissant flakes, bits of cheese and even rice grains often find their way into the crevices of my standard keyboard at work. It gets really disgusting. A few times crumbs got stuck inside the keys and stopped them from working properly. I've used compressed air cans and mini vaccuums but they don't do that great a job. I often end up having to flip the thing over and give it a shake. In addition, I remove all the keys and use a Q-tip to wipe up dust and dirt that get encrusted in these tiny spaces, which is time-consuming.

So you can tell I was relieved to get this washable keyboard. This thing is made for the Oscar Madisons of the world (like me). While you can't use it underwater while scuba diving (the instructions say you shouldn't submerge it in more than 11" of water, and no more than 5 minutes at that), being able to do a wash and rinse (as if it were a dinner plate) is more than enough to get most dirt and crumbs out.

I also like the fact that there is no additional software to install - just plug into the standard USB port, wait a few minutes until your computer recognizes the hardware, and then you're off. The keyboard is about the same size as other computer keyboards, except that the keys feel more like ones you'd find on a laptop. They are round and smooth and make me feel I'm pushing buttons. Because they lay flatter on the surface of the keyboard, you get a softer sound when you type as opposed to the hardier tapping of regular keyboards.

It took me awhile to get used to the feel. The buttons lack the slightly concave ridges that keep your fingers nestled so my fingers felt slippery on them, but not enough to have a problem.

Despite these reservations, however, I think this is a well-made product that is very practical, especially for people like me, who'd rather write than clean. Now all I need is a washable mouse!
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Washable Wired Keyboard K310

Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) My top ten include dogs, sewing machines, houses, my bed, a few trips, and my Kindle. I love my Kindle so much that I actually bought a Kindle edition of a big, heavy, expensive book that I have in hardback just so I don't have to carry it around. It has taken just one month for me to only want to read with the Kindle. It's going to save lots of bookshelf space, my bookshelves are jammed. I love being able to use the dictionary and look up many more words than I used to. Yes, you know the meaning from the context, but it's fun to know the etymology. I took Latin many years ago and frequently consider the root meanings of words, and having the Kindle dictionary makes this easier. Wikipedia is wonderful, too. I looked up the Magna Charta while I was reading a book that mentioned it, and found when it was written, what it was about, etc. I have also looked up some cities to find demographic and weather information.
The ability to change font size and page justification is a good feature. It is important to realize, however, that you can't change justification if the book wasn't formatted to allow that. You get those giant gaps on some lines when it's in full justification. If you use a small font, it's not so bad. Most of the books I have purchased allow left justification, and my guess is that more and more books will be formatted that way, which generally eliminates those gaps. You can get the first chapters of books as free samples, and see how they are formatted, as well as whether you like them as far as writing and subject is concerned.
The next thing I plan to do is put some of my music from my iPod onto the Kindle so I can listen to background music while I read. I understand you can't control the order of the songs, so I'm only going to put on classical music that is not distracting in and of itself.
Getting more books fast is great, too. I forget the name for the phobia that is the fear of running out of things to read, but I have a small case of that, and Kindle is the cure.
Traveling is much nicer when you don't have ten books in your book bag.
I'm asking for an SD card for Christmas from one of the grandkids (it's very inexpensive) so that the Kindle will have even greater capacity.
When you go to the Kindle store from your Kindle, there will be recommendations based on what you have bought, just like there are when you go to Amazon online. However, online you can say "not interested," but on the Kindle, you can't. You get the same recommendations over and over. It would be nice if you could delete recommendations from your Kindle. But, hey, that is definitely just a small thing.
Another thing that would be nice is a password for 1-click ordering from the Kindle.
I'm retired and on a relatively small income. If I lost my Kindle and couldn't afford another one, I would go back to work just long enough to get the money to replace it. That should tell you how much I love it, 'cause I sure don't want to work anymore!
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)
